literal_meaning: Not at all (lit. 'out of ten million')

seo.meta_title: How to Say 'You're Welcome' in Korean | Why Not '천만에요'
seo.meta_description: AI and textbooks teach '천만에요' for 'You're welcome', but Koreans rarely say it. Learn the natural replies: 아니에요, 별말씀을요, 뭘요.

ai_failure.situation: A colleague thanks you for helping move some boxes, and you want to say 'You're welcome.'
ai_failure.ai_mistake: Translates 'You're welcome' as '천만에요', the textbook equivalent.
ai_failure.why_it_fails: 천만에요 is grammatically correct but sounds old-fashioned and theatrical in everyday speech. Koreans usually brush off thanks by denying there's anything to thank them for.

natural_solution.rule: Reply to thanks with 아니에요 (polite default), 별말씀을요 (to elders or in formal settings) or 뭘요 / 아니야 (casual).

alternatives.context: The everyday polite reply — 'No, it's nothing'
More respectful, to someone older or a customer

nuance: English answers thanks by welcoming it ('You're welcome', 'My pleasure'). Korean answers by downplaying the favor: 아니에요 literally means 'It isn't (so)', i.e. 'You don't need to thank me.' That modesty is the point, which is why the textbook phrase — itself a strong denial — sounds overdone when real speakers just shrug it off. Staff in shops may also reply 감사합니다 back, thanking the customer in return.
